description: The English wording of the describe-quantity suite. Same three branches as describe-quantity (on-anchor, item/portion descriptor, grams alone), composed from english-number and english-plural instead of their French counterparts. Two deliberate divergences from the French suite: (1) the rounding-tie case now shows a dot, not a comma; (2) the item-descriptor cases use different counts than the French suite (75 g / 160 g rather than 81 g / 160 g) so the "singular" case actually lands on exactly 1 — 1.1 stays singular in French (count < 2) but would pluralise in English (count != 1), so testing English's own singular boundary needs a count that rounds to exactly 1. Hand-authored: the sandbox stays French-only and has no English reference implementation to generate this from.
generatedBy: hand-authored — sandbox is out of scope, no reference implementation exists

cases.why: Landing exactly on an anchor shows its label, with the exact weight underneath.
Pins the tolerance window: 66 g is 3.1 % from the 64 g anchor, so the clean label is kept rather than degrading to a ratio the moment the user nudges the value.
Pins max(2, grams * 0.04). For a 16 g anchor, 4 % is 0.64 g, which would make the label practically unreachable; the 2 g floor keeps small portions usable.
When two anchors both fall inside tolerance the closer one wins, not the first one scanned.

THE ROUNDING TIE, English side: 80/64 = 1.25 exactly, so round1 evaluates roundHalfUp(12.5)/10 = 1.3 — a dot, not french-number's comma — and 1.3 pluralises in English (unlike French's "1,3 portion", which stays singular under French's count>=2 rule).
Pins the 8 % named window: 100 g is 1.5625 portions, 4.2 % from Large, so the headline reads "≈ Large" rather than a bare ratio.

English's own singular boundary is exactly 1, not "below 2" like French — 75/74 rounds to 1.0, which is the count that must stay singular. No anchors: keeping this case independent of the anchor-tolerance window keeps the arithmetic simple.
At any count but exactly 1 the label pluralises, so english-plural is reachable from this path too, not only from step-label-en.
Below a quarter of an item, "≈ 0.1 carrot" is noise, so the branch is skipped and grams are shown alone. It does NOT fall back to the portion-ratio branch — that is an else-if on the item branch.

Volume foods render "270 mL" — space, capital L — while grams render "64g" with no space; language-independent, since formatWeight's own literals never change with the active language. 270/246 = 1.0975, rounds to 1.1, which pluralises in English.
A weight under 1 g must not render "0g" — language-independent, the same guard as the French suite.
The same guard on the volume side, where the suffix differs.
